EBSCO Research Starters: Palestinians Are Massacred in West Beirut

content.p: For about 43 hours in mid-September 1982, Lebanese Christian militiamen moved through the Palestinian refugee camp of Shatila and the neighbouring district of Sabra in West Beirut. According to Al Jazeera, the killing ran from the evening of 16 September 1982 to the early afternoon of 18 September. The victims were civilians, among them refugees and Lebanese who lived nearby. Israeli troops had surrounded the camps and kept people from leaving. Al Jazeera calls it one of the most traumatic events in Palestinian history, and the questions it raised about who was responsible have been argued over ever since.
content.h2: Background: a camp population and a civil war
content.p: The camps were home to Palestinians who had fled or been driven from their land during the 1948 war that created Israel. Al Jazeera describes the residents of Shatila and Sabra as refugees of the 1948 Nakba. Most lived with few rights. Reset DOC, citing the Kahan Commission's own account, notes that about 270,000 Palestinian refugees were in Lebanon in 1982 by UNRWA's count, and that the Christian armed forces counted nearly twice as many, a figure the commission regarded as an overestimate.

Lebanon's civil war began in 1975. Al Jazeera frames the main fighting as a contest between a Lebanese Front of right-wing Maronite Christian groups, which had Israeli and American backing, and a rival alliance of leftists, Sunni and Shia Muslims and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). The PLO had moved its base to Beirut after 1970. Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982, with the stated aim of destroying the PLO, and its forces under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon besieged Beirut.

The PLO withdrew from Beirut by 1 September 1982. Al Jazeera reports that the United States and a multinational force gave assurances that the remaining Palestinian refugees and civilians would be protected. The force pulled out early, on 10 September.
content.h2: The assassination and the entry into the camps
content.p: On 14 September 1982 Bashir Gemayel, the president-elect, was killed in Beirut. Al Jazeera reports that the Phalange, who blamed the PLO for Gemayel's death, were then let into the camps. The next morning Israel moved into west Beirut and stopped anyone from leaving the refugee camps. Human Rights Watch says that the Israeli army permitted the Phalange militia to enter the camps, where it terrorized the residents for three days. The Kahan Commission record, as Human Rights Watch summarises it, says that Chief of Staff Rafael Eitan testified that the Phalangists' entry into the camps was agreed between Sharon and himself.

Human Rights Watch says the killings were carried out by Phalange members in an area under Israeli Defence Forces control, and that an Israeli forward command post stood on a roof about 200 metres from Shatila. The Christian Science Monitor reported in 2001 that the militiamen had been ordered to cleanse the camps of "terrorists".

The accounts from survivors and reporters describe killings of civilians inside their homes. The Christian Science Monitor, reporting in 2001, recounted the story of one 17-year-old survivor whose father and five siblings were shot dead in her home in Shatila. Human Rights Watch, writing in 2014, says that the dead included infants, children, pregnant women and the elderly, and that some bodies were found to have been mutilated.

Human Rights Watch says the precise civilian death toll most likely will never be known. The figures differ widely. Human Rights Watch gives the Israeli military intelligence estimate as 700 to 800 people killed, and says that Palestinian and other sources have claimed up to several thousand. Al Jazeera gives 2,000 to 3,500 civilians. ABC News, reporting from Beirut in 2002, said that more than 800 people were killed or went missing, and that some estimates put the toll at 1,800. The Christian Science Monitor gave a range of 800 to 2,000 in 2001, and in 2002 wrote that at least 1,000 Palestinians perished. The EBSCO research guide says some reports put the toll as high as 3,500. Each figure should be read with the group that gave it.

The Israeli cabinet set up the Kahan Commission on 26 September 1982, under the Israeli Commission of Inquiry Law. Reset DOC reports that the commission reported in February 1983 and found that Elie Hobeika and Fadi Frem were directly responsible for the killings in the camps. It also found that Israeli leaders were responsible indirectly, for failing to foresee what would happen. Reset DOC names Prime Minister Menachem Begin, Chief of Staff Rafael Eitan, Defence Minister Sharon and others as having failed in different ways. The commission found that neither Mossad nor the intelligence services warned the Israeli defence forces or political leaders that the militia could carry out a massacre if it entered the camps.

The commission's finding on Sharon was the most serious. Human Rights Watch quotes it as saying that the defence minister "bears personal responsibility" for the massacre. It found that the "serious consideration" that the Phalangists were liable to commit atrocities "did not concern [Sharon] in the least", and that his "disregard of the danger of a massacre" was "impossible to justify". The commission recommended that he draw the personal conclusions from his conduct. Sharon resigned as defence minister, though he remained in the cabinet without a portfolio.

The commission did not find that Israel or any Israeli official was directly responsible, because its definition of "direct" responsibility covered only those who carried out the killings. The Middle East Report argues that this distinction does not match international law, under which commanders can be liable for crimes by forces under their control. The UN Security Council condemned the massacres on 19 September 1982. The UN General Assembly later called them an act of genocide. Reset DOC gives the date as 6 December 1982; the Middle East Report gives 16 December 1982. The sources do not agree on the date, so only the year is given here.

The Belgian case began in June 2001. Human Rights Watch says survivors lodged a complaint against Sharon in a Belgian court the day after a BBC documentary on the massacre aired in the United Kingdom on 17 June. The Middle East Report says that on 18 June survivors filed two civil lawsuits. The Christian Science Monitor reported that 28 Palestinian survivors were among the plaintiffs, and ABC News said 23. One of the lawyers who filed the case, Chibli Mallat, is quoted by the Monitor in 2001.

The case relied on a 1993 Belgian law that let local courts hear cases against foreigners suspected of crimes against humanity, no matter where the crimes occurred. A 1999 amendment removed the immunity usually given to serving heads of state, according to the Monitor. Sharon's lawyers argued that he had diplomatic immunity and that a Belgian court had no competence over a crime committed on foreign soil. Sharon had at first dismissed the lawsuit, then hired a Belgian lawyer.

Al Jazeera reports that a Belgian court dismissed the case in 2002 because Sharon was not present in court, even though the 1993 law allowed such trials. According to Human Rights Watch, pressure on Belgium's parliament produced an amendment in April 2003 and a full repeal in August that year, and Belgium's highest court then dropped the case in September 2003. Fox News, reporting on 25 September 2003, said that the court ruled the country no longer had a legal basis to charge Sharon, and that Parliament had amended the law in August to limit complaints to victims or suspects who were Belgian citizens or long-term residents. The dates of the amendment differ between sources; Human Rights Watch gives April for the amendment and August for the repeal.

Elie Hobeika led the Phalange's intelligence wing in 1982, and the Kahan Commission named him among those directly responsible. After Israel withdrew from Beirut he switched his allegiance to Syria, served in several Lebanese governments after the civil war, and later focused on business interests, according to the Monitor. In 2001 he said he was willing to travel to Belgium and testify, and told reporters that he had "evidence that proves my innocence". He did not say what the evidence was.

Hobeika was killed by a car bomb in a Christian suburb of Beirut in January 2002. The Christian Science Monitor reported that he died with three bodyguards, and that no one claimed responsibility. The Monitor reported that most Lebanese immediately accused Israel. Lebanese Minister of Displaced People Marwan Hamadeh said Israel did not want witnesses in the Belgian case. An aide to Sharon, Arnon Perlman, called the accusation "rubbish".

The survivors' accounts were given in interviews years later. ABC News quoted Nadima Nasser, a Sabra resident who lost nearly every male relative in the killings. Suad Srour, who was 17 in 1982, told the Monitor that the Western world "cannot imagine the agonizing moments we went through." Human Rights Watch noted in 2014, after Sharon's death, that he died without facing justice for the massacre, and that the Israeli justice authorities never ran a criminal investigation into the conduct of Sharon or other officers.

Al Jazeera states that not one Lebanese or Israeli fighter or official was punished for the crimes. The camps still house Palestinian refugees who face restrictions on work, property and legal aid. Al Jazeera reports that the UN counts 479,000 Palestinian refugees in Lebanon. Al Jazeera reports that Palestinians commemorate the massacre every year in Lebanon and in Palestine.
